item.content:encoded: In the midst of brilliant scientists, self-sacrificing staff, heroic agents, and even courageous D-class stands… this self-obsessed jerk. I like it! Just a reminder that the Foundation would realistically have idiots in charge who shouldn't be in charge. Solid +1!

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Project Director. Project Manager. GIC. I have found that those with relevant experience/knowledge tend to end up in these positions. Why would you send a team to New England entirely comprised of people from San Diego? The idea is to get the information as efficiently as possible.

So you have an up-and-coming researcher who gets a shot at proving his favorite myth. When things are NOT going well, he starts panicking, and decides they need more time so…make something up! It is unfortunate that this EXACT scenario happens in present-day, peer-reviewed science, and not just in fiction. [http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubble_fusion].

Sometimes, for some people, the desire to find something outweighs the common sense that says "it's not there." Doubly so when you deal with the things the Foundation searches for.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
In my opinion this piece feels a little diminished by everything being spelt out so directly in personal journal entries. One of the charms of SCP articles is that the reader generally has to read between the lines and exercise a bit of interpretation to follow them.

It also seems a little implausible that the director would knowingly set out to commit a wrong-doing and neatly document his culpability like that.

For example, rather than "OMG, I can't believe I falsified records" there could be a memo from the director's office saying "Where's that lab report?", "Here, sorry. The Director wanted some last minute updates". Then when the reader gets to the last sentence the significance of that would click.

Similarly an excerpt from a field report that they've found nothing *again*, (politely) questioning the merit of this particular project and mentioning the mock furry fish on the Director's door in passing (polite) annoyance.

It also seems unlikely that a Director would be selected due to knowledge of the local area. That might be more plausible as a coincidence?

An -EX, which stands for Explained, SCP is one which we have figured out. It is an SCP that is no longer an SCP, either because it has become common place, we worked out the rules behind it, or that it has just become a complete non issue.

item.title: Re: Why did the Foundation ever care?
item.content:encoded:
All of the things you describe would be considered anomalous, though - when they were first discovered. I imagine that the Foundation contains them, studies them, and determines whether the anomaly falls within the bounds of ordinary science. Take flying fish, for example. Foundation gets reports of fish that fly. Sends Agents to investigate. Collects fish, determines that they have no paranormal or inexplicable mechanism and just happen to jump out of the water a lot, and are adapted to doing so. Then they release whatever holds they've placed on flying fish research.

Most such stories would be pretty boring, hence why there aren't a lot of them on the website. But I think it fits pretty well with the Foundation's M.O.

item.title: Why did the Foundation ever care?
item.content:encoded: The problem I have with this is that I can't see why a furred trout would even register as anomalous to the Foundation. There are fish that glow in the dark, fish that walk on land, and fish that fly. There are giant whale-fighting squid, mind controlling parasites, and all kinds of other crazy things. Furry trout? Unless they speak German or travel in time, I'm not really seeing it.

The thing about the trout having a lower than normal body temp makes no sense. Fish are poikilotherms; their body temp is going to be the same as the water. There is no 'normal' temperature.

It also breaks my suspension of disbelief that no one would have figured out it was a fungus. It's pretty easily identifiable on fish. As soon as they put it under a microscope, they'd see it wasn't hair

item.title: (no title)

Forget genetic testing — I personally think it should have been relatively easy to realize that the fur was a fungus without it. I mean, I'm reasonably certain that scientists could tell what a fungus looks like under a microscope in the late '60s / early '70s, even not taking into account how far in advance the Foundation might be.

Also, why would this have been classified as anomalous in the first place? Of interest, certainly, but they wouldn't jump the gun and call it an SCP.

item.content:encoded:
Like this, but given the timeframe the refrence to genetic testing is way out of place and threw me out of the story. While we had models of inheritance, and some idea of the chemical structure of DNA, it wasn't until the mid-50s that we had a proper model for it, and actual genetic testing (as we know it) is much more recent. Just screening for particular genetic diseases wasn't available until the 70s, the kind of technology implied by saying "genetically identical to speckled trout" seems anachronistic, even assuming the Foundation is a decade or two ahead of the rest of the world technologically.

Still, upvote because the idea's good, and aside from the above, I like the execution.
